title: Test day four
hook: notice what you skip: every guest sends an excuse to the great supper, and the host fills the seats anyway
tomorrow: what part of the rule would you miss if it were gone?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: hard. Lehna carried the bundle the sons refused, and the mud was saffron. The week's lines come back in the games: my season, draft one, half, test week, easy, hard. Today, test day four: what got skipped.
screen: `HARD.` → `THE WEEK'S LINES.` → `DAY FOUR: WHAT GOT SKIPPED?`

segments.voice: The invite says maybe, then: can't make it, so sorry. Jesus told a story about that. A man prepares a great supper and invites many. When it's ready, he sends his servant: come, everything is ready. "And they all with one consent began to make excuse. The first said unto him, I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." Another has new oxen to try out. Another has just married. The servant comes back with nothing but apologies. Seat after seat, empty.
screen: `MAYBE. THEN: SO SORRY.` → `A GREAT SUPPER.` → `A FIELD, OXEN, A WEDDING.` → `SEAT AFTER SEAT, EMPTY.`

segments.voice: The host is angry, and then he changes the guest list. Go out quickly, he says, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind. There's still room, the servant says. So go further, out to the highways and hedges, and bring them in, so my house may be filled. Here's the teaching. Jesus tells this at a dinner, right after a guest says how blessed it will be to eat bread in the kingdom of God. Christians read it as a picture of that kingdom: the table is ready now, and the host doesn't cancel the feast. He fills it with people nobody thought to invite. The story ends on a hard line: none of those first invited, the host says, will taste his supper. Notice the excuses, too. None is wicked. A field, oxen, a wedding: all good things, all reasonable, all a way of saying not now. And in the story, not now turns into not at all. That's test day four: notice what you skip, and the reason you give. And here's the week, gathered. My season, named. Draft one, from what was real. Half, the core kept. Test week, begun. Easy, the plain river. Hard, the muddy bundle. And skipped: an empty seat at a supper that's ready now.
screen: `BRING IN THE POOR AND THE BLIND.` · `THERE IS STILL ROOM.` · `GOOD REASONS, STILL NOT NOW.` · `THE WEEK, GATHERED.` · then, large: `SKIPPED.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and walk back through the four days of your test. Find one line you skipped, and the reason you gave it, said plainly, without scolding yourself, the way you'd hear a friend's reason kindly. Then rest in the stillness for the rest of the time: today's supper is still ready.
Test day four: notice what you skip, and the excuse that goes with it. In the parable, the supper is ready now, and the host fills every seat.
Last line of the week: skipped, an empty seat at a supper that's ready now. Day 1694, four days tested.

howItsDone: Christians read the parable of the great supper (Luke 14:15-24) as a picture of the kingdom of God: a supper ready now, which even reasonable excuses turn down, and a table filled with the poor and the overlooked. In a test week, skipped lines and the reasons given are noted without blame.

myth: in the parable, the guests' excuses are wicked or shameful
a field, oxen, a wedding: ordinary, reasonable things. Still, saying not now meant missing the supper.
when the guests refused, the host filled his table with people nobody had invited
the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, from the streets and lanes, then the highways.

fork.setup: your friend skipped her evening walk all week, each time with a good reason. what would the parable have her notice?
options: the excuses themselves: like a field and oxen, good reasons can still mean not now.
that she's a bad person; the parable says every excuse is wicked.
nothing; skipping only matters if someone else is keeping score.
fork.reveal: none of the guests' reasons is wicked; each is a way of saying not now, and they miss the supper. The host's table gets filled anyway.

original.note: Greek: deipnon, the supper of Luke 14.

what it means: in Jesus's parable the excuses are reasonable, the supper is ready now, and the host fills the seats with others; noticing what you skip, and why, is the work.
what a scholar hears: Luke 14:15-24, told at a dinner after a guest says, blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God; Matthew 22 tells a related wedding-feast parable.

chat.meaning: In Jesus's parable the guests gave reasonable excuses, and missed the supper; the host filled the table anyway. Noticing the excuse is the point; tonight's reading is ready now.
